reproduction_number_range.source: Gani and Leach 2004, EID (PMC3323083): about 1.3 before control, geometric offspring distribution

transmissibility_per_day.source: Reproduction number 1.3 divided by the infectious days

case_fatality.source: Gani and Leach 2004 (close to 100 percent) and WHO plague fact sheet (always fatal untreated for pneumonic and septicaemic forms)

immunity.source: Immunity duration is moot: no case survives untreated

stage.latent.source: Gani and Leach 2004: latent mean 4.3 days, SD 1.8, lognormal. Shape 6 is the Erlang with that mean and SD

stage.infectious.source: Gani and Leach 2004: infectious mean 2.5 days, SD 1.2, lognormal. Shape 4 is the Erlang nearest that mean and SD

density_exponent.source: Wikipedia, Basic reproduction number (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basic_reproduction_number, opened): R0 = contact rate / recovery rate, the contact rate set by 'the number of susceptible people in the population that the infected people contact'; whether contact rises with density is not stated there. Chowell et al., 1918 influenza in England and Wales (PMC2596813, opened): 'we found no association between transmissibility, death rates and indicators of population density and residential crowding', R between 1.3 and 1.9, and deaths scaling as population to the power 0.71-0.77 in rural areas and about 1.0 in towns. So the exponent of contact on crowding lies between 0 (that study) and 1 (mass action, density-dependent contact); 0.5 is the midpoint, a ballpark. Rader et al. 2020 (Nature Medicine; search summary only, full text not opened): crowded cities have longer epidemics and larger attack rates.
